html:
A science lesson on your phone may show an animated experiment, play a teacher's voice, pop up a quiz and end with a short video — text, pictures, sound, video and animation working together. That combination is multimedia.

This unit explains each element: how text is styled, how pictures are stored as pixels or as shapes, how sound and video become numbers in a file, and how animation creates movement.

It also shows how to edit images in Pixlr and Canva, sound in Audacity and video in CapCut, the free tools the course uses.

What the SEE asks from this unit (8 marks)

The SEE specification grid gives this unit 8 marks: two MCQs (2 marks), one short question (2 marks) and one long question (4 marks).

MCQs test full forms and "which format for which job" (PNG for lossless web images, WAV for recording your voice, MP4 for video).

The short question is usually two differences — raster and vector, 2D and 3D animation, lossy and lossless — or a definition with an example.

The long question asks for the components of multimedia with their uses, or a scenario such as choosing formats and tools for a school project. Know every full form, and give one example with every point.

3.1 Introduction to multimedia, its elements and applications

Multimedia

Multimedia is the combined use of more than one form of media — text, graphics, audio, video and animation — to present information. Multi means many and media means forms of communication.

The tools and techniques used to create multimedia content such as films, games, websites and learning apps are called multimedia technology.

Apps you already know are multimedia: Duolingo mixes text, voice, sound effects and animation to teach languages; TikTok combines video, filters, text and music; YouTube joins video, sound, thumbnails and live chat; and Google Earth layers satellite images, text labels and 3D maps.

In Nepal, OLE Nepal's E-Paath lessons and the government's Sikai Chautari portal use multimedia for school subjects.

Element What it is Example in a learning app
Text letters, numbers and symbols lesson notes, quiz questions
Graphics still pictures: photos, drawings, charts, icons a labelled diagram of the heart
Audio sound: speech, music, effects the teacher's voice explaining
Video moving pictures recorded with sound a recorded experiment
Animation drawn or computer-made pictures that move an animated water cycle

Multimedia may be linear, playing from start to end like a film, or interactive, where the user clicks, chooses and answers, as in a game or a learning app.

Applications of multimedia

  • Education — e-books, online courses, simulations and quizzes make lessons interactive and easier to understand.
  • Entertainment — films, music, video games and virtual reality.
  • Business and advertising — advertisements, product videos and presentations capture customers' attention.
  • Communication — video calls, video conferencing and social media.
  • Content creation — short videos, graphics and podcasts for social media.
  • Other fields — medical imaging and surgery training, virtual tours for tourism, maps and navigation, news and journalism.
Advantages of multimedia Disadvantages of multimedia
holds attention and makes learning interesting creating good content takes time and skill
explains hard ideas with pictures, sound and motion cameras, computers and software can be costly
suits learners who learn by seeing, hearing or doing large files need storage and fast Internet
allows interaction and immediate feedback too many effects can distract from the message
one presentation can reach a huge audience may not work on old devices or for people without access

Eight applications of multimedia, explained

  1. Education. Animated lessons, e-books and recorded classes make difficult ideas easy to see. Students of Grade 10 watch videos of the heart or of a river forming a delta. Learning apps and the online resources of the Curriculum Development Centre use text, pictures, sound and video together.
  2. Entertainment. Films, music, streaming and computer games are pure multimedia. A Nepali film is shot as video, mixed with audio and given computer-made effects. Millions in Nepal watch songs on YouTube.
  3. Business and advertising. Companies use slide shows, product videos and animated advertisements to attract customers. A bank explains its mobile-banking service in a short animation. This makes the message clear and easy to remember.
  4. Training and simulation. Pilots, drivers and surgeons practise on simulators that combine graphics, sound and movement. A driving-test simulator saves fuel and prevents accidents. Mistakes cost nothing.
  5. Medicine and healthcare. Digital X-rays, CT scans and 3D animation of the body help doctors. Video consultations bring a specialist in Kathmandu to a patient in a hill district. Health-awareness videos on hand washing reach many people.
  6. Journalism and communication. Online news combines text, photographs, video and sound. A report on a flood includes drone video and a map. Video calls let families abroad see their relatives.
  7. Tourism and culture. Virtual tours and 360-degree views of Pashupatinath, Lumbini or the Annapurna trek attract visitors. Museums record old songs and festivals digitally. This keeps culture alive.
  8. Art, design and publishing. Designers make posters and logos with graphics software, and musicians record with audio editors. Magazines, ad agencies and the Nepali digital newspapers all use multimedia tools.

3.2 Text: fonts, typography and text file formats

Text is the characters you see on the screen — letters, digits and symbols, also called alphanumeric characters. It carries most of the exact information in a multimedia product: titles, labels, instructions and explanations.

Text is typed in editors such as Notepad and WordPad and word processors such as Microsoft Word and Google Docs.

Fonts

A typeface is a design of letters, such as Arial; a font is one version of it — a particular size, weight and style, such as Arial Bold 14 point. Font size is measured in points (1 point = 1/72 inch).

Font family Look Examples Best for
Serif small strokes (serifs) at the ends of letters Times New Roman, Georgia printed books and long reading
Sans-serif plain letters without serifs Arial, Calibri, Noto Sans screens, slides, signs
Monospace every letter the same width Courier New, Consolas program code
Script and decorative handwriting or artistic shapes Brush Script titles and cards only

Nepali text should be typed in a Unicode font such as Kalimati, Mangal or Noto Sans Devanagari.

Older non-Unicode fonts such as Preeti store English letters and only draw them as Devanagari, so Preeti text turns into nonsense on any computer or phone that does not have the font.

Typography

Typography is the art of arranging text so that it is easy to read and pleasant to look at.

Its main tools are the choice of font, size and style (bold, italic, underline), colour and contrast with the background, alignment (left, centre, right, justified), line spacing (leading), kerning (the gap between two letters) and hierarchy — making headings larger than body text so the reader sees the structure at a glance.

Typography rules for slides and posters

Use no more than two fonts; a sans-serif font for anything read on a screen; dark text on a light background or the reverse, never red on green; at least 24 point for slide text; and bold, not underline, for emphasis.

Text file formats

Format Full form Stores Notes
TXT Text plain characters only — no fonts, sizes or colours opens in any editor; smallest; used for notes and program code
RTF Rich Text Format text with formatting: fonts, size, colour, bold, alignment, spacing readable by almost every word processor (Microsoft, 1987)
DOCX (Word) Document, XML format text, formatting, tables, images, comments Microsoft Word's own format since Word 2007; actually a zipped bundle of XML files
PDF Portable Document Format text, fonts, images and layout fixed for printing looks the same on every device; used to share final documents

A DOCX file differs from a TXT file in that it keeps the formatting, pictures and tables, needs a word processor to open properly and is larger; a TXT file keeps only the characters.

Worked example 3.1 — how many bytes does text need?

Problem. Plain text in the common UTF-8 code uses 1 byte for each English character and 3 bytes for each Devanagari character. How many bytes does a TXT file need for(a) "Namaste Nepal" and(b) "नमस्ते नेपाल"? (The Devanagari phrase is made of 11 Unicode characters plus one space.)

Solution.(a) "Namaste Nepal" has 13 characters including the space, so 13 bytes.(b) 11 Devanagari characters × 3 bytes + 1 space × 1 byte = 33 + 1 = 34 bytes. Python confirms both: len("नमस्ते नेपाल".encode("utf-8")) returns 34.

3.3 Graphics: raster and vector, pixels and resolution, formats, and editing

Graphics are the visual elements of multimedia: photographs, drawings, charts, logos, icons and shapes.

They are made and edited in programs such as Pixlr, Canva, GIMP and Adobe Photoshop (for photos) and Inkscape and Adobe Illustrator (for drawings and logos). A computer stores a picture in one of two completely different ways.

Raster graphics, pixels and resolution

Raster graphics and pixel

A raster (or bitmap) image is a grid of tiny squares called pixels.

A pixel (short for picture element) is the smallest unit of an image shown on a screen; each pixel holds one colour, usually as three numbers for its red, green and blue (RGB) light, each from 0 to 255.

The resolution of a raster image is its number of pixels, written as width × height, for example 1920 × 1080. More pixels show more detail but make a larger file.

For printing, resolution is also given as pixels per inch (ppi) or dots per inch (dpi): about 300 ppi gives a sharp photo print.

The colour depth is the number of bits per pixel: 24-bit colour (8 bits each for red, green and blue) gives about 16.7 million colours. When a raster image is enlarged, the pixels become visible as blocks — pixelation.

Vector graphics

Vector graphics

A vector image stores a picture as shapes described by mathematics: points (anchors), straight lines, curves (Bézier curves), and their fill and outline colours. The computer redraws the shapes at whatever size is needed, so a vector image stays sharp at any size.

Raster (bitmap) graphics Vector graphics
made of a grid of pixels made of mathematically described points, lines and curves
blurs or pixelates when enlarged stays sharp at any size
file size grows with the number of pixels file size grows with the number of shapes; usually small
best for photographs and realistic images best for logos, icons, diagrams, fonts, maps
edited pixel by pixel (Pixlr, Photoshop, GIMP) edited shape by shape (Inkscape, Illustrator)
formats: JPG, PNG, GIF, BMP, WebP formats: SVG, AI, EPS (and PDF)

Graphics file formats

Most image formats compress the pixel data to make files smaller. Lossless compression rebuilds every pixel exactly; lossy compression throws away detail the eye is unlikely to notice, giving much smaller files.

Format Full form Type Key features Typical use
JPG / JPEG Joint Photographic Experts Group raster, lossy small files for photographs; quality setting; no transparency camera photos, web photos
PNG Portable Network Graphics raster, lossless supports transparency; sharp edges and text stay crisp logos on websites, screenshots, diagrams
GIF Graphics Interchange Format raster, lossless but only 256 colours simple animation; on/off transparency short animations, stickers
WebP (Web Picture) raster, lossy or lossless smaller than JPG and PNG; transparency and animation modern websites
BMP Bitmap raster, uncompressed very large files old Windows programs
SVG Scalable Vector Graphics vector sharp at any size; text-based icons, logos, maps on websites
PDF Portable Document Format document (raster and vector) fixed layout, prints identically sharing and printing documents and posters
GIF is not the only animated image format

GIF is often remembered as the classic animated image format, though WebP and APNG (animated PNG) also store animations, usually in better quality and smaller files than GIF; GIF is simply the oldest and most widely supported.

Worked example 3.2 — pixels, bytes and print size

Problem.(a) How many pixels are in a 1920 × 1080 image, and how many bytes does it need uncompressed at 24-bit colour?(b) A 3000 × 2000 photo is printed at 300 ppi. How large is the print?(c) Simplify the ratio 1920 : 1080.

Solution.(a) 1920 × 1080 = 2,073,600 pixels. 24 bits = 3 bytes per pixel, so 2,073,600 × 3 = 6,220,800 bytes, about 6.2 MB.(b) Width = 3000 ÷ 300 = 10 inches (25.4 cm); height = 2000 ÷ 300 = 6.67 inches (16.9 cm).(c) The highest common factor of 1920 and 1080 is 120; 1920 ÷ 120 = 16 and 1080 ÷ 120 = 9, so the aspect ratio is 16 : 9.

Worked example 3.3 — choosing the format

Problem. Choose a format for each and give the reason:(a) the school logo with a transparent background for the website;(b) the same logo for a 6-metre banner;(c) photos from the school sports day for the Facebook page;(d) a small looping "Thank you" animation;(e) the final exam routine for parents.

Solution.(a) PNG — lossless with transparency.(b) SVG (or another vector format) — vector graphics stay sharp when enlarged to banner size.(c) JPG — photographs compress well and load quickly.(d) GIF (or animated WebP) — supports simple animation.(e) PDF — the layout looks the same on every phone and printer and is not easily edited.

Editing images in Pixlr

Pixlr is a free online image editor at pixlr.com, with an app for phones. The quick editor formerly called Pixlr X is now named Pixlr Express, and the advanced one Pixlr Editor.

Its workspace has four areas: the canvas (where the image is shown and edited), the tools panel (left), the layers panel (right) and the navigation tools for zoom, pan and rotate.

Task Steps in Pixlr
New project Open pixlr.com → Pixlr Express → Create new → choose a preset or type a name and size (e.g. 1920 × 1080) → Create
Add text Text tool (T) → Add new text → type → change font, size, colour, alignment and spacing in the left panel; drag the handles to resize, the round dot to rotate
Add a shape Arrange (or Elements) → Shape → choose square, circle and so on → set fill, outline and shadow
Work with layers Layers panel → + to add a layer → the ⋯ menu to rename, hide, lock or change opacity and blend mode → drag to reorder
Insert a photo Element / Add media → choose the file → Open
Cut out an object Cutout tool → choose shape, softness or the Draw and Lasso cutout → drag over the object → Keep or Remove to refine
Export Save → choose the name, format (JPG, PNG, WEBP or PXZ) and quality → Save as

PXZ is Pixlr's own layered format: save in PXZ to keep layers for later editing, and export a PNG or JPG for sharing. A higher quality setting gives a sharper image and a bigger file.

Designing in Canva

Canva (canva.com, with a phone app) is a free online design tool built around templates.

Choose the kind of design (poster, presentation, Instagram post, certificate), pick a template, then replace its text and pictures by dragging Elements (shapes, icons, stickers, photos) on to the page.

Uploads brings in your own images, Text adds headings, and Share → Download exports the design as PNG, JPG, PDF or, for animated designs, MP4.

Pixlr is better for editing a photograph itself; Canva is faster for laying out a poster, card or presentation from ready-made parts.

Activity 1.1 — create and edit a graphic

Open a photo in Pixlr (or Photoshop). Put the background, the photo and a title on separate layers; select one area and change only it; add a shape, text and one filter; then export the result as PNG and as JPG at quality 70.

Compare the two file sizes and the sharpness of the text, and present your image to the class.

3.4 Audio: digital sound, audio file formats, and recording and editing

Audio is the sound in multimedia: speech, music, instruments and sound effects. Sound is a vibration that travels through air as a pressure wave.

A microphone turns the wave into a changing electrical voltage (an analogue signal), and the computer's sound card turns that into numbers.

From sound wave to digital audio

An audio waveform is the graph of a sound against time. Its amplitude (height) shows the loudness; the time taken by one complete wave is its period, and the number of waves each second is the frequency, which we hear as pitch (high or low).

Width on a waveform is time, not wavelength

On a waveform graph drawn against time, the width of one wave is its period; wavelength is a distance in metres. What matters for sound is the frequency (frequency = 1 ÷ period), which sets the pitch.

To store sound, the computer measures the wave at regular instants — sampling — and stores each measurement as a number:

  • the sampling rate is the number of samples per second; music CDs use 44,100 Hz (44.1 kHz) and video uses 48 kHz;
  • the bit depth is the number of bits per sample; 16-bit audio has 65,536 possible levels;
  • the number of channels: 1 for mono, 2 for stereo.

The size of uncompressed audio follows directly:

\text{size in bits} = \text{sampling rate} \times \text{bit depth} \times \text{channels} \times \text{seconds}

Worked example 3.4 — WAV against MP3

Problem. Find the size of one minute of CD-quality stereo audio (44.1 kHz, 16-bit, 2 channels) stored as WAV, and of the same minute as a 128 kbps MP3. How many times smaller is the MP3?

Solution. WAV: 44,100 × 16 × 2 × 60 = 84,672,000 bits; ÷ 8 = 10,584,000 bytes ≈ 10.6 MB. MP3: 128,000 bits per second × 60 s = 7,680,000 bits; ÷ 8 = 960,000 bytes = 0.96 MB. Ratio = 10,584,000 ÷ 960,000 ≈ 11 times smaller.

This is why songs are shared as MP3 or AAC but recorded and edited as WAV.

Audio file formats

Format Full form Compression Features and use
WAV Waveform Audio File Format none (uncompressed) exact copy of the recording; very large; used for recording and editing
MP3 MPEG-1 Audio Layer III lossy small files, plays everywhere; made portable music players and streaming possible
AAC Advanced Audio Coding lossy better quality than MP3 at the same bit rate; used by YouTube, iPhones and Android
M4A MPEG-4 Audio lossy (usually AAC) AAC sound in an MP4 container
FLAC Free Lossless Audio Codec lossless about half the size of WAV with no loss
OGG Ogg Vorbis lossy free, open format used in games

The bit rate (kbps) of a compressed file sets its quality and size: 128 kbps is fine for speech and casual listening; 192–320 kbps sounds close to the original.

Recording and editing audio in Audacity

Audacity is a free, open-source audio editor for Windows, macOS and Linux (audacityteam.org). Its window has a menu bar, a toolbar with the transport buttons, a timeline across the top, one track for each recording showing its waveform, and level meters.

Task Steps in Audacity
Record plug in a microphone and choose it in Audio Setup; press the red Record button (or R), speak, and press Stop (or Space)
Import a file File → Import → Audio, or drag the file into the window
Cut out a part drag across the unwanted part of the waveform to select it, then Edit → Delete (or press Delete)
Apply an effect select a part and open the Effect menu, where effects are grouped: Fading → Fade In / Fade Out, Volume and Compression → Amplify / Normalize, Noise Removal and Repair → Noise Reduction, Delay and Reverb → Echo; preview, then apply
Listen press Play (Space); the play head moves along the timeline
Export File → Export Audio, give a name, choose MP3 or WAV, the quality (bit rate) and channels, then Export

AudioMass (audiomass.co) is a free audio editor that runs directly in the browser.

It works the same way: its menu bar, waveform display and control panel offer Record (press R and choose the microphone), File → Load from Computer, select-and-scissors to cut, an Effects menu (normalize, fade in, fade out, reverse, pitch shift, and reverb with time, decay and wet settings), and File → Export/Download as MP3 or WAV with a chosen bit rate.

Activity 1.2 — record and edit a clip

Record a 30-second introduction of yourself in Audacity or AudioMass. Remove a cough or a long pause, add a short fade in and fade out, use Normalize so the volume is even, and export it once as WAV and once as 128 kbps MP3.

Compare the two file sizes with the formula above, then play both to the class.

3.5 Video: frames, frame rate and resolution, formats, and editing

Video and frame

Video is a series of still pictures called frames, shown one after another so quickly that the eye sees continuous motion, usually together with a sound track. The number of frames shown each second is the frame rate, measured in frames per second (fps).

A higher frame rate gives smoother motion and a larger file:

Frame rate Where it is used
24 fps cinema films
25 fps television in Nepal, India and Europe (the PAL standard)
30 fps television in the USA (NTSC), most online video and phones
50–60 fps sports, video games, slow-motion and smooth phone video

Resolution is the number of pixels in each frame, width × height. The aspect ratio is the ratio of width to height: 16 : 9 for TV and YouTube, 9 : 16 for vertical TikTok and Reels, 4 : 3 for old TVs.

Name Resolution Pixels per frame Common use
SD (Standard Definition) 720 × 480 (720 × 576 in PAL countries) 345,600 old TVs, DVDs
HD 1280 × 720 921,600 online video on slow connections
FHD (Full HD) 1920 × 1080 2,073,600 TVs, laptops, YouTube, phone cameras
4K UHD 3840 × 2160 8,294,400 large TVs, films, high-end phones

Worked example 3.5 — why video must be compressed

Problem.(a) How many bytes does one uncompressed Full HD frame need at 24-bit colour, and how many per second at 30 fps?(b) The same video is saved as an MP4 at 8 Mbps. How big is a 10-minute video?(c) How many frames does a 90-minute film at 24 fps contain?

Solution.(a) 1920 × 1080 × 3 bytes = 6,220,800 bytes per frame; × 30 = 186,624,000 bytes, about 187 MB every second (11.2 GB a minute).(b) 8,000,000 bits × 600 s = 4,800,000,000 bits; ÷ 8 = 600,000,000 bytes = 600 MB. Compression (by a codec such as H.264) makes the video about 300 times smaller.(c) 24 × 90 × 60 = 129,600 frames.

Video file formats

A video file is a container that holds the compressed video, the audio and extra data such as subtitles. The way the pictures are compressed is the codec (H.264, H.265, AV1).

Format Full form Features and use
MP4 MPEG-4 Part 14 the most widely used; good compression with H.264 or H.265 video and AAC audio; plays on phones, YouTube, Netflix
MOV QuickTime Movie Apple's format, compressed or uncompressed; used on iPhones and Macs and in editing
AVI Audio Video Interleave Microsoft's older format (1992); large files; compressed or uncompressed
MKV Matroska Video free open container; many audio and subtitle tracks
WebM Web Media open format for the web, used by YouTube in browsers

Editing and exporting video in CapCut

CapCut is a free video editor from ByteDance, used online at capcut.com, on Windows and Mac, and as a phone app (some effects are paid).

Clipchamp, built into Windows 11, and the open-source Shotcut and Kdenlive are free alternatives that work the same way: every editor has a media area, a preview, a timeline and an export button.

Task Steps in CapCut
New project capcut.com → Create new video → choose the aspect ratio (16 : 9 for YouTube, 9 : 16 for TikTok) → click "Untitled project" to rename it
Import Media → Upload → From this device → select the files → Open; they appear in the media area
Arrange click a clip, or drag it, on to the timeline; drag clips to change their order; use the zoom slider to see detail
Play press Space or the play button; the play head (cursor) moves along the timeline
Trim drag the start or end handle of a clip to shorten it
Split and delete move the play head to the cut point → Split → select the unwanted piece → Delete
Transition hover between two clips → Add transition → choose one → drag its edges to change its length
Effects and filters Effects panel → place the play head → click an effect → double-click it on the timeline to adjust
Text Text → Add heading → type → set font and colour in Properties → drag the text clip's edges to set how long it shows
Export Export → Download → choose the resolution (e.g. 1080p), frame rate (e.g. 30 fps) and quality → Export; the file is an MP4
Activity 1.3 — comparing SD, HD and FHD

Watch the same clip in SD, HD and FHD and fill in the table.

Resolution Dimensions Picture quality File size Common use
SD 720 × 480 soft; detail and small text blur on a big screen smallest old TVs, very slow mobile data
HD 1280 × 720 clear on a phone about 2.7 × SD (more pixels) online video, phones
FHD 1920 × 1080 sharp, fine detail about 6 × SD (more pixels) TVs, laptops, YouTube, games

Reflection. FHD shows the most detail because it has the most pixels. Upload a school project at 1080p (FHD) so it is sharp, and let viewers choose a lower quality. On limited mobile data, HD or even SD saves data.

Films and modern games use FHD or higher because large screens make every pixel visible.

Activity 1.4 — edit a short video

Import three or four clips into CapCut or Clipchamp, arrange and trim them, add a transition between each pair, a title and one filter, then export the video as a 1080p MP4 and present it.

3.6 Concept of animation

Animation

Animation is the illusion of movement created by showing a series of slightly different drawings or computer images quickly one after another. In multimedia it usually means computer animation, made with software.

Animation is used for cartoons, films, advertisements, video games, websites and learning materials. 2D and 3D describe how the pictures are made; frame-by-frame and keyframe describe how the movement is made.

2D animation is flat: its pictures have only width and height. Each frame is drawn, or characters are built from flat parts that move. Cartoons, explainer videos, animated stickers and many advertisements are 2D.

Free 2D tools include Pencil2D, OpenToonz and Krita; Adobe Animate is a common paid one.

3D animation has width, height and depth, so objects have volume and can be seen from any angle with light and shadow.

A character is first modelled (built as a 3D mesh), then rigged (given a skeleton of joints), textured, animated by moving the rig, and finally rendered into frames.

Pixar's Toy Story (1995) was the first feature film made entirely with computer animation. Blender is a free 3D tool; Maya and 3ds Max are professional ones.

2D animation 3D animation
two dimensions: width and height three dimensions: width, height and depth
flat look depth, perspective, light and shadow
drawn frame by frame or built from flat parts modelled, rigged, textured, animated, rendered
quicker and cheaper to make needs more skill, time and computing power
cartoons, stickers, explainer videos animated films, games, architecture walkthroughs
Pencil2D, OpenToonz, Adobe Animate Blender, Maya, 3ds Max

Frame-by-frame animation: the animator draws every frame separately. It gives full control and a hand-made look, but it is slow: one second of film at 24 fps needs 24 drawings.

Keyframe animation: the animator sets only the important positions — the keyframes, such as the start and the end of a movement — and the software calculates the frames in between, called in-betweens or tweens (the process is tweening).

Almost all computer animation today is keyframed.

Worked example 3.6 — counting the drawings

Problem. A ball rolls across the screen in 2 seconds at 24 fps. How many frames are there? How many must the animator make by hand(a) frame by frame and(b) with keyframes at the start and the end?

Solution. Frames = 24 × 2 = 48.(a) Frame by frame: all 48 drawings.(b) Keyframes: 2 positions; the software produces the other 48 − 2 = 46 in-betweens.

Where animation is used: films and cartoons; video games; advertisements and logos that move; education (an animated heart pumping, the water cycle, E-Paath lessons); websites and apps (loading icons, stickers, emojis); science, medicine and engineering simulations; architecture walkthroughs; and weather maps on television.

Animation and psychology. Animators use what attracts people's attention: bright colours and movement catch the eye, which is why cartoons for children are colourful and busy; expressive faces help viewers feel for a character; and well-timed, smooth movement makes an animation pleasant and easy to follow.

Activity 1.5 — find the elements

Watch a multimedia presentation or website chosen by your teacher. List every example of text, graphics, audio, video and animation you can find, then discuss in class how each one helps the message.

1. Full forms. (i) RTF — Rich Text Format. (ii) PNG — Portable Network Graphics. (iii) GIF — Graphics Interchange Format. (iv) JPG — Joint Photographic (Experts) Group. (v) SVG — Scalable Vector Graphics.

(vi) PDF — Portable Document Format. (vii) MP3 — MPEG-1 Audio Layer III (MPEG Audio Layer 3). (viii) AAC — Advanced Audio Coding. (ix) MP4 — MPEG-4 Part 14. (x) AVI — Audio Video Interleave.

2. Multiple choice — answers

i. (b) — multi means many: many types of media.

ii. (a) — cost and access to hardware and software is a drawback; the others are benefits.

iii. (b) — TXT stores only the characters.

iv. (c) — the characters on screen are text.

v. (b) — vector graphics are built from Bézier curves and scale without loss.

vi. (b) — a PDF can hold raster and vector graphics and is used to share documents.

vii. (c) — amplitude (height) is loudness.

viii. (c) — MP3 is the common compressed format for sharing.

ix. (c) — resolution is the number of pixels, width × height.

xi. (a) — width, height and depth.

3. Short notes — model answers

a. Components of multimedia. Multimedia has five components: text (written information), graphics (still images such as photos, drawings and charts), audio (speech, music, effects), video (recorded moving pictures with sound) and animation (drawn or computer-made pictures that move). Together they make information interesting and easy to understand.

b. Rich Text Format. RTF is a text file format created by Microsoft (1987) that stores text together with its formatting — fonts, sizes, colours, bold and italic, alignment, indentation and line spacing.

Almost every word processor can open it, so it is used to exchange formatted documents.

c. Audio waveform. A waveform is the graph of a sound against time. Its height (amplitude) shows loudness and the number of waves per second (frequency) shows pitch.

To store it, the computer samples the wave thousands of times a second (44,100 for CD sound) and saves each value as a number.

d. Video resolution and frame rate. Resolution is the number of pixels in each frame, written width × height — SD 720 × 480, HD 1280 × 720, FHD 1920 × 1080; more pixels give a sharper picture and a bigger file.

Frame rate is the number of frames shown each second (fps) — 24, 25, 30, 50 or 60; a higher rate gives smoother motion.

e. Raster and vector graphics. Raster graphics are grids of pixels, best for photographs, and they pixelate when enlarged (JPG, PNG, GIF). Vector graphics are shapes described mathematically, best for logos and icons, and stay sharp at any size (SVG, AI, EPS).

f. 2D and 3D animation. 2D animation is flat, with width and height only, and is usually drawn frame by frame (cartoons). 3D animation has width, height and depth; models are built, rigged and moved, then rendered (Toy Story, games).

4. Questions — model answers

a. Text, graphics, audio, video and animation.

b. A raster graphic is an image made of a grid of pixels, each with its own colour; its quality depends on the number of pixels (resolution).

c. JPG (JPEG), PNG and GIF (also BMP and WebP).

d. Raster images are made of pixels and lose quality when enlarged; vector images are made of mathematical shapes and stay sharp at any size. Raster suits photos, vector suits logos and diagrams, and vector files are usually smaller.

e. In education multimedia makes lessons interactive and easier to understand through pictures, sound, video and simulations, and lets students learn at their own pace.

In business it attracts customers through advertisements and product videos, explains products clearly, and helps companies communicate through presentations and video meetings.

f. A TXT file stores only plain characters, opens in any editor and is very small. A DOCX file stores text with fonts, colours, tables, images and page layout, needs a word processor, and is larger.

g. For a greeting card: text for the message and names, graphics for a photo, border and decorations, and, for a digital card, a little animation (falling flowers, a glowing diya) and audio (a short tune) to make it lively and personal.

h. PNG — it is lossless and supports a transparent background, so the logo sits cleanly on any colour. (SVG is even better on websites because it stays sharp at every size.)

i. Vector — a billboard is enlarged many times, and a vector design is redrawn sharply at any size, while a raster image would pixelate unless it had an enormous number of pixels.

j.

Similarities both combine several media, are interactive and are used for learning.

Differences YouTube centres on video with sound, text titles and thumbnails, and is used to watch and share content; Google Earth centres on satellite images and 3D maps with text labels, and is used to explore places.

YouTube is mostly linear viewing; Google Earth is exploration the user controls.

k. A learning-app screen could have: a text title and short notes (exact information), a labelled graphic (shows structure at a glance), an audio button to hear the explanation (helps reading and pronunciation), a short video of a real experiment, an animation of the process (makes motion and change clear), and a quiz with instant feedback (interaction).

Sketch them as boxes on one screen: title at the top, image and video in the middle, audio and quiz buttons at the bottom.

l. Video combines moving pictures, sound and text, so it shows processes and emotions that text or audio alone cannot, holds attention and is easy to understand for people of every reading level — which is why most Internet traffic today is video.

But video files are large, need more data and better devices, take longer to produce and are hard to skim or search; text is quicker to scan and audio can be heard while doing something else.

The best choice depends on the message, the audience and their connection.

Chapter summary

  • Multimedia combines text, graphics, audio, video and animation; it may be linear or interactive and is used in education, entertainment, business, communication and content creation.
  • Text: serif, sans-serif and monospace fonts, size in points; typography arranges text for readability. Formats: TXT (plain), RTF (formatted), DOCX (Word), PDF (fixed layout). Use Unicode fonts for Nepali.
  • Raster images are grids of pixels (JPG, PNG, GIF, BMP, WebP) and pixelate when enlarged; vector images are mathematical shapes (SVG, AI, EPS) and stay sharp. Raw size = width × height × bytes per pixel.
  • Lossless compression keeps every detail (PNG, FLAC); lossy throws some away for small files (JPG, MP3, MP4).
  • Audio: amplitude = loudness, frequency = pitch; sampled at, e.g., 44,100 Hz with 16 bits. Size = rate × bits × channels × seconds. WAV is uncompressed; MP3 and AAC are compressed.
  • Video = frames shown at a frame rate (24, 25, 30, 60 fps) with a resolution (SD 720 × 480, HD 1280 × 720, FHD 1920 × 1080). Formats: MP4, MOV, AVI, MKV.
  • Tools: Pixlr (photo editing, layers, cutout; JPG/PNG/WEBP/PXZ), Canva (templates), Audacity/AudioMass (record, cut, effects, export), CapCut (timeline, trim, split, transitions, text, export MP4).
  • Animation: 2D (width, height) and 3D (with depth: model, rig, animate, render); frame-by-frame draws every frame, keyframe animation draws key poses and the software makes the tweens.

Answers to Group B

1. Raster graphics are made of pixels and lose quality when enlarged; vector graphics are mathematical shapes and stay sharp at any size. Raster suits photographs (JPG, PNG); vector suits logos and diagrams (SVG).

2. A pixel (picture element) is the smallest dot of an image, holding one colour. 1280 × 720 means the image is 1280 pixels wide and 720 pixels high — 921,600 pixels in all (HD).

3. 44,100 × 16 × 2 × 30 = 42,336,000 bits; ÷ 8 = 5,292,000 bytes ≈ 5.3 MB.

4. Lossless compression makes a file smaller without losing any detail, so the original can be rebuilt exactly (PNG, FLAC). Lossy compression throws away detail that is hard to notice, giving much smaller files (JPG, MP3, MP4).

5. Frame rate is the number of frames shown each second (fps). Sports are full of fast movement; 50 or 60 frames per second show each movement in more steps, so the ball and players look smooth instead of jerky.

6. 2D animation has width and height only and looks flat; 3D animation adds depth, perspective, light and shadow. 2D is drawn or built from flat parts; 3D is modelled, rigged and rendered, and needs more time and computing power.

7. In keyframe animation the animator sets only the key positions (start, end, important poses) and the software calculates the frames in between (tweening). In frame-by-frame animation every frame is drawn by hand, which gives full control but takes far longer.

8.(a) MP3 (or AAC) — small file that plays on every phone.(b) PDF — keeps the layout, prints identically and is not easily changed (a JPG is also acceptable for a photo of it).

Model answer D1: multimedia, elements and applications (10 marks)

Introduction. Multimedia is the combined use of more than one medium, namely text, graphics, audio, video and animation, controlled by a computer and usually interactive. A web page with a news story, a photograph and a video clip is multimedia.

Elements.

  1. Text: words in fonts, in headings, captions and menus (TXT, DOCX, PDF).
  2. Graphics (images): photographs, drawings and logos (JPG, PNG, SVG).
  3. Audio: voice, music and sound effects (MP3, WAV).
  4. Video: moving pictures of real events with sound (MP4, AVI).
  5. Animation: drawn or computer-made pictures that appear to move (GIF, SWF).

Applications. Education, entertainment, business and advertising, training and simulation, medicine, journalism, tourism and art and design.

Advantages Disadvantages
Explains ideas clearly with sound and pictures Needs a costly computer with large memory
Interactive, so learning is active Files are large and slow to download
Attracts and holds attention Takes time and skill to produce
Many media in one place Needs software and hardware that may be outdated
Easy to update and share Too many effects can distract from the message

Conclusion. Multimedia is powerful because several senses are engaged at once, so it is used in classrooms, hospitals, newsrooms and film studios.

Model answer D2: raster and vector graphics (10 marks)

Introduction. A computer stores a picture either as a grid of coloured dots or as a list of shapes, which gives two types: raster (bitmap) and vector graphics.

Terms. A pixel (picture element) is the smallest dot of a raster image. Resolution is the number of pixels in an image, such as 1920 × 1080, or the density of dots in dots per inch (dpi).

Colour depth is the number of bits per pixel; 24 bits gives about 16.7 million colours.

Point Raster graphics Vector graphics
Made of Pixels Lines, curves and shapes defined by formulas
Quality on enlarging Becomes blurred or blocky Stays sharp at any size
File size Large for high resolution Small
Best for Photographs Logos, maps, diagrams
Formats JPG, PNG, GIF, BMP SVG, AI, CDR, EPS
Software Photoshop, GIMP Illustrator, Inkscape, CorelDRAW

Formats. JPG is lossy and gives small files for photographs. PNG is lossless and supports transparency. GIF has 256 colours and simple animation. BMP is uncompressed. SVG is a vector format for the web.

Size calculation. An uncompressed picture of 1600 × 1200 pixels in 24-bit colour needs 1600 \times 1200 \times 3 = 5{,}760{,}000 bytes, about 5.76 MB; JPG compression can reduce it to under 1 MB. An 800 × 600 picture needs 1.44 MB.

Conclusion. Choose raster for photographs and vector for logos, since only vector keeps clean edges when enlarged on a banner.

Model answer D3: audio, video and animation (10 marks)

Introduction. Digital sound and moving pictures must be converted from the real world into numbers.

Audio. Sound is an analogue wave. The computer samples it many times per second and stores each sample with a certain number of bits.

Sampling rate is the number of samples per second (CD quality is 44,100 Hz), and bit depth is the bits per sample (16). Formats: MP3 (lossy, small), WAV (uncompressed), MIDI (instructions for notes), OGG. Editors: Audacity.

One minute of CD-quality stereo needs 44100 \times 16 \times 2 \times 60 / 8 = 10{,}584{,}000 bytes, about 10.6 MB.

Video. A video is a sequence of still pictures called frames shown quickly, with sound. Frame rate is the frames per second (fps): cinema uses 24, television 25 or 30. Resolution is 1280 × 720 (HD) or 1920 × 1080 (Full HD).

A raw Full HD frame is 1920 \times 1080 \times 3 = 6{,}220{,}800 bytes, so at 25 fps one second is about 155 MB, which is why video is compressed. Formats: MP4, AVI, MKV, MOV. Editors: Kdenlive, CapCut, Premiere Pro.

Muybridge's horse photographs of 1878 showed that a quick series of pictures gives the illusion of movement.

Animation. Animation is the illusion of motion made by showing drawn or computer-made pictures in rapid sequence. Types: traditional (cel), 2D, 3D and stop motion.

It works because of persistence of vision, the eye's keeping an image for about 1/16 of a second. Formats: GIF, SWF, MP4.

Point Audio Video Animation
Content Sound Real moving pictures Drawn or computed pictures
Key term Sampling rate Frame rate Frames, tweening
Formats MP3, WAV MP4, AVI GIF, SWF
Software Audacity Kdenlive Blender, Synfig

Conclusion. Audio, video and animation all become numbers in a computer, and compression keeps their large files manageable.
